items.title: Liesman: Why Greenspan could bet on productivity — and Warsh needs to hike
items.summary: Alan Greenspan famously held the line on interest rates because he believed in the productivity promise of the internet boom. Why can't Kevin Warsh do the same?
items.body: In a discussion on CNBC's Halftime Report Wednesday, the question came up: Why can't Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh hold the line on interest rates the way his icon Alan Greenspan did at the beginning of the dot-com era? Greenspan famously leaned against inflation hawks on his committee in 1995 and 1996, holding the line on interest rates amid strong growth, because he believed in the productivity promise of the internet revolution. It would be nice if Warsh could follow the same playbook amid the artificial intelligence build-out and keep rates steady until the productivity arrives. Unfortunately, a quick look at the numbers shows just how different the situation is for Warsh when it comes to inflation , the magnitude of the capital-investment boom and the monetary and fiscal stimulus boosting the economy.

items.title: Nvidia's billion-dollar board bet: Who's protected as lawsuits mount?
items.summary: Nvidia's board is under investigation, and directors are already defendants in a shareholder lawsuit accusing them of failing to properly oversee the company.
items.body: Jensen Huang is back as CEO of Nvidia , after President Donald Trump urged the company's board to rehire Huang. But investigations into the company, its executive leadership and its board continue as outside criticism mounts. "Clearly they caved to external pressure," said Betsy Atkins, an author and longtime public-company director. "The board failed," she said, when it initially allowed Huang's removal. "The board's role is to think of all stakeholders." California Attorney General Rob Bonta is investigating whether Nvidia misrepresented information to investors. "There is classic corporate securities law on the books in California that prevents investors and the public from being misled by companies," Bonta said on CNBC's " Squawk on the Street " on Tuesday. Directors are already defendants in a shareholder lawsuit accusing them of failing to oversee Nvidia.

items.title: Poundland collapses putting 11,000 jobs at risk
items.summary: The discount chain has fallen into administration after its owners failed to find a buyer.
items.body: Poundland has collapsed into administration, putting 11,000 jobs at risk, after its owners failed to find a buyer to keep it in business. The retailer's shops and distribution centres will remain open and continue to trade during the administration process with the business likely to be broken up and some of its stores sold off to rival retailers. Poundland's US owners held talks with several bidders over a last-minute rescue deal, but no agreement was reached. Poundland boss Barry Williams said in a note to staff that the board had "no alternative but to take this decision", but was making it with "sincere sadness and intense regret". He said the US owners Gordon Brothers had removed "all borrowing facilities and access to our bank accounts" on 27 October, and adequate funds had not been released since then to keep the business solvent.

items.title: German firms eye Africa as global trade shocks hit traditional markets
items.summary: German businesses are optimistic about Africa, but Berlin's cautious approach to risk is holding them back from cashing in on the opportunities that their competitors from countries like the UAE and Turkey are seizing.
items.body: "Africa is a land of opportunity." "The German-African relationship is a win-win." "The continent is the market of the future." That's what many business leaders and politicians have to say about Africa at the sixth edition of the German-African Business Summit in Accra, Ghana. While these descriptions aren't new, there's a palpable sense of urgency and seriousness this time. German firms are increasingly viewing Africa as an attractive destination as they scramble to find new markets amid wars in Ukraine and Iran, high energy prices, punishing US tariffs and slowing growth in traditional markets like China. "For a long time, many German companies had a secure source of revenue from the major export markets in North America and China, but the geopolitical ruptures of our time have undermined this certainty," German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier said during the event.

items.title: ECB and Sveriges Riksbank conclude agreement for Sweden to join T2
items.body: The European Central Bank (ECB) and Sveriges Riksbank have concluded an agreement for Sweden to join T2, the Eurosystem’s real-time gross settlement system. Today, ECB President Christine Lagarde and Sveriges Riksbank Governor Erik Thedéen took part in a signing ceremony for the T2 currency participation agreement at the ECB. This agreement will enable Sveriges Riksbank to use T2 for settling large-value payments in Swedish kronor. Migration is targeted for February 2030. Joining T2 will move Sweden’s large-value payment settlement from a national platform to shared European infrastructure. Sveriges Riksbank and Swedish financial institutions will benefit from investments in security, resilience and technological development that are shared across participating markets, as well as from common European standards.

items.title: Tech stocks sink but close well off the lows, Anthropic struggles to rebound above IPO price
items.summary: Nvidia and other AI-linked stocks fell as investors weighed AI spending, inflation and higher-rate risks.
items.body: Technology stocks fell on Wednesday as excitement over Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang 's return faded and failed to calm concerns over the sustainability of the artificial intelligence trade. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite declined 0.6% and traded off its lows, recovering from steeper losses earlier in the session. Semiconductor stocks dragged on the index, and the VanEck Semiconductor ETF that tracks the sector edged down 1%. "We just feel that this is panic right now," Venu Krishna, head of U.S. equity strategy at Barclays, told CNBC's " Squawk on the Street " on Wednesday. "What the market is telling you is that the AI growth narrative has hit a wall and given the centrality of that theme at the economic level, the market is expecting some sort of a macro shock," he added. After notching one of its best days on record Monday, Nvidia has fallen in the days since and slumped 4% Wednesday.

items.title: Fed’s preferred inflation gauge accelerated to 3.8% in October, raising the 2027 stakes for the central bank
items.summary: The personal consumption expenditures price index was expected to show an annual inflation rate of 3.8% in October, according to the Dow Jones consensus.
items.body: Inflation moved further away from the Federal Reserve's target in October, reinforcing expectations that another interest rate hike is in the cards for December and raising questions about how much more work the central bank will have to do in 2027. The personal consumption expenditures price index , the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, showed a seasonally adjusted 3.8% annual inflation rate, in line with the Dow Jones consensus estimate and nearly twice the central bank's goal. The reading was 0.1 percentage point higher than September. Excluding food and energy, core PCE was 3.3%, the Commerce Department reported Wednesday. That was 0.1 percentage point above the forecast. While the Fed officially follows the headline figure, policymakers consider core to be a more reliable longer-term gauge of inflation trends.

items.title: AI debt markets shudder as Nvidia's top 'banker' returns
items.summary: Fears about some companies' AI debt ramped higher Tuesday, a day after Jensen Huang's return as Nvidia CEO.
items.body: Fears about the massive debt being taken on to fund the artificial intelligence buildout climbed Tuesday as Wall Street weighed what Huang's return to Nvidia means for its bankrolling of the AI boom. Huang is considered one of the top financiers, or bankers, in the AI industry, spearheading deals with neoclouds like CoreWeave and other firms to buy chips, backed in some cases by Nvidia guarantees. His return to Nvidia has revived prospects for the company to continue "circular financing" of AI chips and data centers — raising concerns among credit investors. CoreWeave, which has become the poster child of AI debt concerns, saw its stock sink 13% and the yield on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 top 17%. Bond yields move inversely to prices. At the same time, the spread on the neocloud company's five-year credit default swaps jumped 8.5% to over 1,200 basis points.

items.title: UK food inflation could hit 5% next year, Bank of England says
items.summary: Sharp rise expected as cost pressures mount, with experts factoring in energy price cap hike and potential impact of El Niño Food price inflation in the UK could hit 5% next year, the Bank of England has said, despite rising less sharply than feared since the onset of the Iran…
items.body: Food price inflation in the UK could hit 5% next year, the Bank of England has said, despite rising less sharply than feared since the onset of the Iran war. The deputy governor Clare Lombardelli told MPs on the cross-party Treasury select committee: “Food price inflation is coming in under what we expected [it] to be, and in fact under what the industry expected it to be.” But she said the Bank expected food price inflation to rise sharply from the current level of about 1.3%. “We think that … it will go up to 3 to 5% in the middle of next year. I mean, obviously that’s quite uncertain, but that pressure is there,” Lombardelli said. Lombardelli was being questioned by MPs alongside other members of the Bank’s monetary policy committee (MPC).

items.title: German auto workers on back foot as costs, competition bite
items.summary: German auto workers profited during the industry's boom years, but are now increasingly being asked to trade past gains for future job security.
items.body: For decades, German auto bosses and labor representatives touted their ability to work through their disagreements in a uniquely cooperative process. Those days appear to be gone. A series of crises across the industry and abrupt moves by management to slash costs are testing the limits of the German power-sharing agreement. As negotiations between union representatives and Germany's largest carmaker, Volkswagen, began on Tuesday, the balance of power appeared increasingly one-sided. Volkswagen wants to freeze wages for the next two years while cutting several allowances and bonuses. Alongside Mercedes , it's demanding longer hours under the same pay, with both companies threatening to withhold investment from German factories. Unions have responded with warning strikes and the threat of larger walkouts.

items.title: Card payments edge past cash in shops; euro area consumers want both
items.body: The European Central Bank (ECB) today published its latest study on the payment attitudes of consumers in the euro area (SPACE). The results show that consumers are increasingly using digital means of payment, while cash continues to play an important role. For the first time since comparable data were collected in 2016, [ 1 ] cards were used more often than cash at physical locations, such as shops. In 2026 cards accounted for 45% of transactions, compared with 44% for cash. Mobile payments increased to 9%, from 6% in 2024. While payment practices are changing, consumers’ own preferences remain stable. When paying in a shop, 54% preferred cards or other cashless methods, 22% preferred cash and 23% had no clear preference. A large majority of respondents attach importance to retaining a choice of payment methods.

items.title: U.S. proposes new tariffs on 14 trading partners, including China and the EU
items.summary: The new levies seek to counter foreign trade practices deemed unfair, discriminatory or burdensome to U.S. commerce.
items.body: The U.S. is preparing new tariffs on 14 economies , including China, the EU, Japan and India, following investigations into what the Trump administration says are excess manufacturing practices that disadvantage U.S. commerce. The administration launched those and other trade investigations in March , weeks after the Supreme Court unraveled a major piece of President Donald Trump 's tariff-heavy economic policy by striking down his "liberation day" duties. Trump has since been accused by critics of his tariffs of trying to revive the canceled duties using other legal authorities. The latest action targets foreign economies that create, sustain or contribute to structural excess capacity and production in manufacturing sectors that the U.S. finds unreasonable and burdensome or restrictive to its commerce, a senior U.S. official told reporters Tuesday evening.

items.title: Even the price of toys is on the rise. How Americans are scaling back holiday plans
items.summary: U.S. consumers face higher food, travel and gift costs in 2026 as inflation and Iran-war energy shocks pressure holiday budgets.
items.body: As Amanda Brecht planned how her family would spend Thanksgiving this year, she had to make some difficult decisions. Because of high gas prices , the 30-year-old decided she wouldn't drive across her home state of Michigan to celebrate with extended family. Instead, Brecht and her husband will spend the holiday with just their three kids. And with food prices rising, they'll be skipping appetizers and serving turkey breast instead of a whole bird. "Thanksgiving is definitely going to look different this year," Brecht said. "Money doesn't grow on trees. You can only do so much." With inflation accelerating, Americans like Brecht will see higher prices almost everywhere they look this holiday season . At a time of year synonymous with food, gifts and big spending, many consumers are instead pinching pennies, paring back their plans and making tough choices about how they'll celebrate.

items.title: Kalshi daily volume of ‘perps’ trading begins to top its prediction markets
items.summary: The product, the first one beyond event contracts, was introduced in May.
items.body: Kalshi is known for its prediction markets across sports , politics and culture . But now, for the first time, perpetual futures, Kalshi's second financial product, has surpassed the notional trading volume of its event contracts on consecutive days. On Thursday, perpetual futures — commonly known as "perps" — on Kalshi saw $3.4 billion in notional volume as artificial intelligence laboratory Anthropic stock debuted on public markets while the rest of the market sold off . That exceeded about $3 billion in notional volume for Kalshi's prediction markets on the same day. Perps are futures-style contracts where there is no expiration and traders do not need to own the underlying asset. Contracts instead continuously track the price of an asset, with funding payments to keep the contract price aligned with that of the market.

items.title: US announces new tariffs on host of countries including China
items.summary: The new levies would hit many of America's biggest trading partners, including China and the EU.
items.body: The US has announced a fresh raft of tariffs as President Donald Trump pushes ahead with his signature trade policy. The new taxes charged on imports to America are set to hit many of the country's biggest trading partners - China, the European Union and 12 other jurisdictions. The move follows the White House's investigation into the trade practices of other countries in March after the US Supreme Court ruled Trump's previously announced Liberation Day tariffs were illegal . China is facing the highest rate of up to 40%, followed by Vietnam at up to 35% and then others facing either 20% or 25%. Tariffs are taxes levied on imported goods. The amount is typically calculated as a percentage of the good's value and paid to the government by businesses importing the products from abroad. Some of these rates will be effectively reduced because of caps on tariffs Trump has agreed to.

But investors are now starting to ask harder questions about the bill for the AI build-out — and demanding evidence that the huge spending is actually adding value for shareholders, according to Dan Taylor, deputy chief investment officer and CIO equities, systematic at Man Group .

items.title: ‘Ready for any storm’: UAE minister optimistic on economy as IMF lifts forecast
items.summary: The UAE is optimistic about achieving 7%-8% economic growth next year, banking on a "different" economic model.
items.body: The UAE is "very optimistic" about achieving 7%-8% growth next year, the country's economy and tourism minister Abdulla bin Touq Al Marri told CNBC after the latest data from the International Monetary Fund showed the country would avoid a recession in 2026. The IMF last week revised the UAE's real GDP forecast to 0.2% growth in 2026 from a 3.9% contraction predicted a month ago . "The UAE is coming back, and that adjustment within one month shows that there is a huge potential aspect when it comes towards the end of the year," the minister told CNBC's Dan Murphy . He said the tourism industry was already picking up with occupancy rates returning to "almost near normal" and international carriers including British Airways and Air France rerouting flights to the UAE. The minister expects economic growth to be higher than 0.2% this year.

items.title: US stocks fall further as fears over AI intensify
items.summary: All three main US indexes were down in early trading, with the tech-dominated Nasdaq down almost 4%.
items.body: Big technology firms connected to AI continued to see share prices fall on Wednesday, with stock in Nvidia and Anthropic dropping sharply in early trading. The surge in Nvidia shares after boss Jensen Huang was reinstated was temporary, and the general stock sell-off continued, with all three main US stock market indices down by closing time. The tech-dominated Nasdaq closed 0.6% lower. The declines came amid concerns over the level and sustainability of AI investment, which has rattled investors in recent weeks. Shares in other major tech firms, including Amazon, Tesla and Microsoft closed the day lower, though Meta and SpaceX were in positive territory by the end of the trading day. Nvidia's share price was down 8% in early trading on Wednesday, extending Tuesday's slide as the boost from Huang's return eased. At close, it ended up 3.4% lower.

items.title: Stick or switch? UK billpayers weigh up how to beat January energy jump
items.summary: Despite dozens of fixed deals lower than next Ofgem price cap, many customers argue savings do not justify the risk Energy bills in Great Britain to rise 26% in January “I’m looking at the off-peak rate more than doubling, peak increasing considerably as well as the standing…
items.body: “I’m looking at the off-peak rate more than doubling, peak increasing considerably as well as the standing charge,” says Andy, who lives on Scotland’s west coast. “I have an electric vehicle and an air-source heat pump and use a lot of off-peak energy. I’d like to stay with Octopus Energy … but there are better-looking deals out there.” The retired woodworker is among the millions facing a jump in energy bills when the price cap in Great Britain rises by 26% in January. He says he “got lucky” last time with a “very good” 12-month deal, but it ends next month. The new cap, set by the regulator Ofgem , works out at £2,166 for a typical annual gas and electricity bill – up £443 on the October to December equivalent. Yet, even though there are dozens of deals available to fix for less, two-thirds of households remain on the default tariff that tracks the cap.

items.title: Consumer confidence shoots up after Democrats' midterm victories — though inflation worries persist
items.summary: The Conference Board survey released Tuesday showed improvement across the board, with the headline confidence index jumping to 103.3.
items.body: Consumers grew significantly more optimistic in November in the wake of the midterm elections , with a growing number of Americans now seeing improvement in the labor market and expecting inflation to cool. The Conference Board survey released Tuesday showed improvement across the board, with the headline confidence index jumping to 103.3, up 11.4 points from October and much better than the Dow Jones consensus forecast for 92.2. Confidence among Democrats and independent voters improved sharply, the Conference Board said, while confidence among Republican respondents fell slightly. Still, confidence among Republicans remained the highest among the three groups. While respondents "continued to express frustration with high prices and rising costs," they also "cited hope for the general economy," said Fergus McCormick, the board's senior economist for global indicators.

items.title: Energy bills to rise by 26% from January after gas prices surge
items.summary: A household using a typical amount of energy would see its annual bill rise from £1,723 to £2,166 if this level was sustained for a year.
items.body: Energy bills will soar by 26% for millions of households in January after a surge in gas prices sparked by the Iran war. A typical bill will increase by about £37 a month in the first three months of the new year, although the price will depend on how much energy a household uses, so it could be closer to £60 extra a month in winter. A household using a typical amount of energy in England, Scotland and Wales and paying by direct debit, would see their annual bill rise from £1,723 to £2,166 if the increase was sustained for a year, said regulator Ofgem. The government will pay millions of households £100 from 4 January to help cover winter costs on top of an existing VAT cut on electricity. Charities and suppliers expect debt to rise and a wave of people to need emergency support.

items.title: Amazon to start selling cars in the UK next year
items.summary: US retail giant links up with Hyundai in attempt to crack £200bn British market Amazon is planning to sell cars in the UK from early next year, in a move that threatens to disrupt the vehicle retail market. The Amazon Autos service will be launched in “early 2027”, starting with…
items.body: Amazon is planning to sell cars in the UK from early next year, in a move that threatens to disrupt the vehicle retail market. The Amazon Autos service will be launched in “early 2027”, starting with cars from the Korean manufacturer Hyundai. It will be the first time the US tech company has sold cars outside its home country. Amazon, which is the world’s biggest online retailer with a market value of $2.7tn (£2.1tn), started selling cars at the end of 2024 in an effort to expand into one of the few remaining major consumer markets it had not already targeted. Its latest move will be watched closely by car retailers that share a UK market worth more than £200bn a year. Amazon Autos operates in 150 US cities and counts thousands of dealers in its networks, offering vehicles from 35 brands.

items.title: Liesman: Nvidia whiplash tests Kevin Warsh’s push to read market signals
items.summary: The extreme market gyrations and the drama surrounding Nvidia this past week have highlighted the dilemma facing Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh.
items.body: The extreme market gyrations and the drama surrounding Nvidia this past week have highlighted the dilemma facing Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh . On Friday, as stocks sold off, market-based probabilities that the Fed would raise interest rates declined. On Monday, with Jensen Huang back in office , a powerful rally restored market confidence that two more rate hikes are coming. On one level, ignoring daily market vicissitudes and focusing on the long term is at the heart of one of the key changes Warsh wants to push through at the Fed. On another, he has been explicit that markets do a better job of forecasting and he wants to use market indicators more than forecasts to guide policy. Take the benchmark Goldman Sachs Financial Conditions Index.

items.title: Why tiny cars are taking off across Europe
items.summary: Once seen as a car for elderly, rural people, tiny cars are being embraced by a younger demographic.
items.body: Selena Buse, 16, reverses her Citroën Ami out of a parking space and heads off past the school playground. Heads turn. The Ami looks pretty remarkable. Futurist or like-a-toaster depending on your point of view. But it's changed her life. "I got it because I really needed it to get to school. And I use it to visit friends on the weekends. It's indispensable in rural areas like where I live," she says. In France, you can drive a car like this from the age of 14 with a road safety certificate and eight hours training. In Italy too. In Germany and Spain it's 15, in the UK 16 , external . Because they are classed as motorised quadri-cycles. Four-wheel mopeds in other words. Registrations have risen from about 13,000 in 2019 to around 25,000 last year in France. In Europe, sales have gone from 30,000 to 60,000 in the past five years.

items.title: EasyJet boss unable to rule out further job losses after profits collapse by 96%
items.summary: Kenton Jarvis says rival airlines could go bust after Iran war drives sharp rises in fuel prices and hits travel demand The boss of easyJet has said he cannot rule out further job cuts and predicted some rival airlines could go bust, after soaring fuel prices this year triggered…
items.body: The boss of easyJet has said he cannot rule out further job cuts and predicted some rival airlines could go bust, after soaring fuel prices this year triggered a collapse in profits. EasyJet’s pre-tax profit dropped 96% to £24m in its financial year ending in September, compared with £658m in the previous 12 months. The airline, which has agreed to a £5.7bn takeover by the US private equity firm Apollo , said in July it had lost more money than expected during the spring, as the Iran war pushed up fuel prices and hit travel demand . Kenton Jarvis, the chief executive of easyJet, said on Wednesday that the year was “challenging for airlines due to the Middle East conflict and its effect on demand and fuel prices, which materially impacted our financial performance”. This month, it emerged that the airline was consulting on cutting up to 50 roles at its head office in Luton.

items.title: Budget carrier Norse Atlantic falls 78% after warning its finances are ‘critical’ amid soaring fuel costs
items.summary: The Norwegian low-cost carrier said its situation is dependent on securing financing for its short-term liquidity needs.
items.body: Norse Atlantic shares plummeted Wednesday after it revealed the company is in a "critical financial situation" as soaring fuel costs amid the Iran war strain budget carriers during the winter season. The Norwegian low-cost carrier said its situation is dependent on securing financing for its short-term liquidity needs. The company has had discussions about a potential strategic takeover as well as other options including ACMI contracts, which refer to short-term capacity leasing. "Norse is also engaged in discussions with selected parties on short term financing, however, there can be no assurances that such discussions will result in a viable solution," it added. The start of the U.S.-Iran war on Feb. 28 sent jet fuel prices soaring, putting pressure on airlines around the world. Prices are now up nearly 72% to $155 per barrel year-on-year as of the week ending Nov.

items.body: Donald Trump's investment portfolios have bought or sold shares in chipmaker Nvidia at least 44 times this year, a review of the US president's financial disclosures shows. Trump's most recent public declarations of his investment trading show that between January and September the portfolios purchased between $5.2m and $17m (£4m and £13m) in Nvidia stock - and sold between $4.4m and $12m. His portfolios held between $12.5m and $58m of Nvidia shares at the end of 2025. Rossi wrote that “when one of the largest members of the FTSE 100 concludes that its interests are better served elsewhere, policymakers cannot regard it as an isolated corporate decision.” “ The continued departure of major companies from London’s stock market should concern anyone who cares about Britain’s economic future,” he said.

items.body: Domestic energy prices will soar by 26% in January under the regulator Ofgem's new price cap, pushing up bills for millions of households across England, Scotland and Wales. With household budgets already under pressure, finding ways to reduce gas and electricity costs has become increasingly important. But how much difference can simple changes really make? The BBC spoke to three people about what they're doing to keep their energy costs down. Like many people, Kelly Anne Harvey, a building surveyor from Cleveleys near Blackpool, is worried about her energy bill going up next year. The 44-year-old, who is married with a five-year-old son, has a combined household income of £60,000. items.title: What will the energy cap changes mean for my bills?
items.summary: Regulator Ofgem is raising the cap affecting the energy bills of millions of households.
items.body: Energy bills are to soar in January, as prices governed by regulator Ofgem's cap rise at the coldest time of the year. The cap affects millions of people in England, Scotland and Wales, and reflects higher wholesale gas costs which have been pushed up by the US-Israel war with Iran. It means people on variable tariffs should give an accurate meter reading, ensure they are receiving all the support to which they are entitled, and take care over energy use. The energy cap fixes the maximum amount which customers on standard variable tariffs can be charged for each unit of gas and electricity used. It covers more than 20 million households in England, Wales and Scotland and is set by the regulator Ofgem every three months , external . It affects those paying by direct debit, by standard credit (they pay when they get a bill), or prepayment meters in slightly different ways.

items.body: S hocked by average annual energy bills at £2,166 for the first three months of next year? Here’s worse news. It is currently possible, and perhaps even likely, that the regulator, Ofgem, will set the price cap at £2,000-plus in every quarter of 2027. Predictions for bills are less certain the further out one looks, it should be said. Gas prices, the overwhelming culprit in the £443 hike in the cap announced on Wednesday, can always fall – and might do so if calm returns to the strait of Hormuz. But EDF’s outlook for next year currently reads: £2,254 for the second quarter, which will include about £100 extra in the “network costs” line in bills that includes paying for the upgrade of the electricity grid – demonstrating that gas prices are not the only story on a medium and long-term horizon. Then £2,078 in the quarter starting in July and £2,035 from October.

items.body: A sk Andy Burnham a question and it won’t be long before he mentions the cost of living. Responding to the results of midterm elections in the US earlier this month, he said that the Democratic party’s triumph meant that there was “an opportunity now to unite around the issue that is affecting us all, and that’s the cost of living”. This wasn’t a non sequitur. The Republicans lost control of Congress in large part because Donald Trump failed to address concerns about the cost of basic goods – a failing aggravated by the US president’s disastrous war against Iran, which caused a spike in commodity prices, exacerbating the affordability problem. Mr Burnham correctly identified the transmission mechanism by which geopolitical problems feed domestic political resentment.

items.title: Our ‘Paris manifesto’ proposes how to deal with extreme wealth in the AI age | Open letter
items.summary: It is possible for democracy to reverse the dynamic of oligarchy. But we must act now The explosion of extreme wealth in the world is the defining social fact of our times. When Forbes magazine began ranking the world’s largest fortunes in 1987, the wealth of the richest 0.0001%…
items.body: The explosion of extreme wealth in the world is the defining social fact of our times. When Forbes magazine began ranking the world’s largest fortunes in 1987, the wealth of the richest 0.0001% of our planet’s population equaled 3% of global GDP. Since that time, the wealth held by this tiny group of people – just 3,000 households – has ballooned and now reaches 17% of global GDP. This extreme wealth explosion has upended the balance of power, leaving choices that affect all of humanity to a few billionaires at the helm of a handful of corporations. The economic power of the ultra-wealthy is being used to consolidate their political power, creating a dynamic that is threatening democracy. This dynamic of wealth and power is nothing new (the word “oligarchy” comes from ancient Greek), but its velocity and the scale of its cross-border impacts are unprecedented.

items.body: Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis hit Saudi Arabian sovereign wealth fund Public Investment Fund Tower on Tuesday, injuring 11. The kingdom's civil defense directorate did not name the tower, but posted an image showing damage to the PIF tower. Eyewitness reports by Al Jazeera also indicated that the building that was hit was the PIF Tower in Riyadh. The injured included two Saudi citizens, two Indians, three Nepalis, and four Egyptians. The attack comes as tensions have flared up again between Saudi Arabia, which is leading an international coalition to restore the internationally recognized government of Yemen after it was forced to flee in 2015, and the Houthis. Turki al-Maliki , a spokesperson for the coalition, said one of the towers of the financial center was targeted in a "cowardly terrorist attack," referring to the financial center in the Saudi capital of Riyadh.

items.title: AI's shock-and-awe raid on maths looks like pride before a fall | Rafael Behr
items.summary: Machines are bulldozing through hard problems to assert the power of their tech bro creators, not to advance human knowledge In most walks of life, trying something 12,363,153,437,138 times and getting the same result is reason enough to assume it works every time. Not in maths,…
items.body: I n most walks of life, trying something 12,363,153,437,138 times and getting the same result is reason enough to assume it works every time. Not in maths, where a conjecture that holds up more than 12tn times looks very probably true but doesn’t qualify as proven. That was the status of the Riemann hypothesis, one of the most famous mathematical conundrums in existence, until last week . Then Levent Alpöge, a mathematician working at Anthropic, said he and his collaborator, Claude AI, had crossed the line from conjecture to proof. I don’t pretend to understand much of what Bernhard Riemann proposed in 1859. I know it relates to primes – whole integers greater than 1 that are divisible only by 1 and themselves – and the pattern of their distribution along the infinite number line.

items.title: What’s the most sustainable way to eat fish? Forget it. There isn’t one | George Monbiot
items.summary: Don’t take the bait offered up by ‘conservation’ charities. Fishing is about as good for our ecosystems as tobacco is for our health Drumroll please. I am about to unveil the species of fish that’s best to eat if you want to protect the living seas. Ta-dah! It’s … I hope that…
items.body: D rumroll please. I am about to unveil the species of fish that’s best to eat if you want to protect the living seas. Ta-dah! It’s … I hope that clears things up. Unfortunately, over the past few years, a noisy industry has developed to tell you otherwise. You’re doing the planet a favour if you eat mackerel , sorry, cod, I mean haddock, no coley, make that pollack – oh, whoops! These choices might make you feel better about yourself. But they do nothing but harm to marine wildlife. The fish you should choose is none of the above. Cause, could I introduce you to effect? In April, the Marine Conservation Society, through its Good Fish Guide, suggested you stop eating cod and eat hake instead . Six months later, it lamented that hake is now overexploited thanks to “increased fishing pressure” , and downgraded its sustainability ratings. How on earth did that happen? Beats me.

items.body: Defence lawyer Brian Heberlig makes closing arguments at the Huawei Technologies trial at Brooklyn federal court on November 17. Huawei has been found guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud, but not guilty of the more serious overarching racketeering charge in a landmark case in the US. In a two-month trial, prosecutors accused the Chinese technology and telecommunications giant of lying, cheating and stealing to gain any competitive advantage. Huawei's defence team argued that prosecutors had decided Huawei was a criminal organisation and built its case from there, but the firm's success was due to its own innovation. Huawei said , external the racketeering acquittal "confirms that these allegations lack factual basis", adding that it would "take all necessary legal actions to defend our rights and interests".

items.body: The contract caterer switching to New York is a big hit to the London Stock Exchange but what is being done to discourage others from delisting? T hat’s gratitude, eh? Compass Group built its business, in part, on contracts to serve dinners in British schools and run catering operations in NHS hospitals. Now it plans to switch its primary stock market listing to New York in 2028. Compass is a bad one for the London market to lose. First, it is the 18th largest company in the FTSE 100 index and one of the few that is the biggest in the world in its market (contract catering, not just for the public sector but for thousands of corporate clients). Second, its reasons for joining the stateside listing rush feel flimsy – but also dangerous.

The verdict marks a major development in a long-running criminal case against Huawei, with charges first publicly disclosed in 2019. A federal jury found Huawei and three of its subsidiaries guilty of multiple offenses, including bank and wire fraud and conspiracy to commit money laundering, the Justice Department said in a statement. "No person or company is above the law," U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche said, accusing Huawei and its subsidiaries of conducting business in the United States through deception and theft.

items.body: Newcastle United’s owner, Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF), is looking to sell up to 25% of the club by issuing new shares. The New York-based bank JP Morgan, whose most recent involvement in a major football deal was Fifa’s aborted attempt to sell off 20% of its commercial rights last summer, has been appointed to handle the sale, as first reported by the Athletic . PIF is seeking investment partners to help fund major infrastructure projects, such as building a new stadium or redeveloping St James’ Park, and would dilute its shareholding rather than profiting from the proceeds of the share issue. The state-owned fund owns 84% of Newcastle after the departure of the minority shareholder Amanda Staveley two years ago, with the remaining 16% owned by the London-based Reuben brothers.

items.title: Trump open to pardoning Jensen Huang if needed: NY Post
items.summary: Trump said he would be willing to pardon Jensen Huang if needed and argued that the Nvidia CEO should not have to invoke the Fifth Amendment before Congress.
items.body: President Donald Trump said he would be willing to pardon reinstated Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang if needed after Huang appears before Congress next week, according to an exclusive interview with the New York Post. Huang's reinstatement followed Trump's intervention with Nvidia's board, including a reported call into a board meeting to argue for his return. Even so, lawmakers are still set to scrutinize his relationship with suspected Chinese intelligence asset Alice Huang in two appearances next week. Nvidia shares surged 31% on Monday after Huang was reinstated as CEO, before falling 5.9% on Tuesday amid a broader market pullback. Trump also said that Huang should not need to invoke the Fifth Amendment to avoid self-incrimination when he appears for a closed-door interview with the House Foreign Affairs Committee on Dec. 1 and before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 3.

items.title: ‘It’s been really a mess’: Meta insiders concerned over push to AI content moderation
items.summary: Several employees say rapid speed at which algorithms work means mistakes can happen at greater scale Meta employees have expressed concern at the company’s push to replace human moderators with artificial intelligence, claiming the technology is leading to mistakes with the…
items.body: Meta employees have expressed concern at the company’s push to replace human moderators with artificial intelligence, claiming the technology is leading to mistakes with the potential for sweeping political consequences. The social media company, which owns Facebook and Instagram, has been experimenting with AI-driven moderation for years, first introducing it in 2017 to filter out violent extremist content. This March, Meta announced it was “transforming our approach” by rolling out “more advanced AI systems” to moderate content across its apps, framing the change as a way to improve enforcement. Several Meta employees said that behind the scenes this push to AI was accompanied by mass layoffs across the company, severely affecting staff responsible for reviewing content on its platforms.

items.title: China’s Xiamen Airlines to buy 50 Boeing jets in $7.4 billion deal
items.summary: Xiamen Airlines has agreed to purchase 50 Boeing 737-8 aircraft with a combined catalog price of around $7.4 billion.
items.body: China Southern Airlines said in a filing late Tuesday that its subsidiary Xiamen Airlines had agreed to purchase 50 Boeing 737-8 aircraft with a combined catalog price of approximately $7.4 billion. The announcement comes after President Donald Trump told CNBC on Monday that he expected China to purchase another 250 Boeing aircraft, following his meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping at the APEC summit last week. "By the way, I sold 250 Boeings to China, and I think they're going to do another 250," Trump said. In May, China approved an initial purchase of 200 Boeing aircraft for Chinese airlines following Trump's visit to Beijing, marking the country's first commitment to purchase U.S.-made Boeing aircraft since 2017, according to the White House. It was not immediately clear whether Xiamen Airlines' latest purchase was part of that commitment.

items.title: Japanese companies shift away from ESG-linked executive pay
items.body: TOKYO -- The share of Japanese companies that tie executive compensation to environmental, social and governance targets declined this year for the first time in data going back to 2021, as businesses increasingly favor investor-focused metrics like capital efficiency.
